subject: CPLT
course_description: This course draws on classical, modern, and contemporary texts to introduce skills required for reading comparatively across national traditions and academic disciplines with an emphasis on close reading, critical interpretation, and the multiplicity of linguistic traditions around the world. *Note: This course is non-repeatable.
course_notes: (Topic: Death, Art, and Immortality) Great artists boast that their work will outlast the "devouring tooth" of time, that they might overcome death through art. This course explores such claims through a close consideration of literature that thematizes the quest for immortality. This will challenge us to contemplate our own relation to death, but our attitude will not be bleak. By engaging art, literature, and philosophy, we'll discover the resources within us to face life's impending end bravely, beautifully, and creatively. After reading Virginia Woolf's "The Death of the Moth" and Tolstoy's novella to set the tone, our study will begin by wrestling with different perspectives on immortality: the religious ideas of the Bible and the Upanishads, the psychology of Otto Rank, and the philosophies of Nietzsche and Heidegger. Then we'll take an Orphic plunge into the connection between death, artist and artwork, reading classic poems alongside reflections from Blanchot and Proust. For the rest, we'll devote our time to short stories by authors like Yourcenar, Borges and Poe, novels by Bioy Casares, Dick, and Hrabal, and a play by Samuel Beckett. All tackle our theme from uniquely exhilarating angles, spanning the grave to the hilarious, always pleasurable and thought-provoking. We'll discuss photography, the loss of worlds, life as a dream, the ordeal of art-working, the thinness of the veil between life and death, and what it might mean to become immortal through devotion to truth in art. How does confronting our mortality inspire us to art? What does the artistic vocation cost? What can preservation technologies really hold of who we are? What fills the gap where art fails? This class will appeal to anyone who has a creative vocation, values the creative word, and/or just loves great literature and wants to think through essential questions of life and mortality together. Class discussions will be lively and intense. Assignments to include weekly reflections, book presentations, a music playlist project, and a final essay or creative project. Required Texts: Leo Tolstoy, The Death of Ivan Ilyich Adolfo Bioy Casares, The Invention of Morel Philip K. Dick, Ubik Bohumil Hrabal, Too Loud a Solitude Roland Barthes, Camera Lucida
